html:
Ceylon tea is the tea of Sri Lanka, whose plantation trade began in 1867 when the Scottish planter James Taylor planted a field of tea on the Loolecondera estate near Kandy.

At the time the island's hill country was covered in coffee estates. Then the fungus behind coffee rust struck from 1869, and over the next two decades the coffee crop collapsed. Planters tore out their bushes and put in tea, using seed from Assam. By the 1890s tea had replaced coffee.

The trade grew fast:

  • Planters brought in Tamil labourers from south India, the Tamil workers to Ceylon estates, who lived in crowded estate lines.
  • Thomas Lipton bought estates in 1890 and sold cheap packaged tea in Britain.
  • Colombo grew into a tea auction centre.

Tea became the backbone of the colony's economy. After independence the estates were nationalised in the 1970s and later handed to private firms. The country took the name Sri Lanka in 1972, but kept "Ceylon tea" as its brand. It remains among the world's top tea exporters, along with India, Kenya and China.
sum: Ceylon tea is the tea of Sri Lanka, whose plantation trade began in 1867 when the Scottish planter James Taylor planted a field of tea on the Loolecondera estate near Kandy.
